articleTitle: Ozone generation by pulsed corona discharge in a wire cylinder arrangement
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: In general, the aim in an ozone generator is to produce intense corona discharges without inducing full breakdown between the electrodes, The dielectric barrier in the conventional set up inhibits such breakdown. There are other possibilities, however. If the electric field is made highly nonuniform, as in a point/plane or wire/cylinder arrangement, for example, then the low field region close to the plane or cylinder essentially acts, for times less than the crossing times for charged particles, as a charge collector in much the same way as the dielectric barrier. If a generator could be devised on this basis, it would contain no fragile dielectric and, as such, would be intrinsically more reliable. The project to which this paper relates aims, amongst other things, to explore the factors controlling the ozone generation rate in a wire/cylinder geometry. The authors describe the experiments conducted and their results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: Hospital waste has been found to contain 20% plastic by weight, around 4 times than in municipal waste. Pre-packaged nonrecyclable materials lead to a large amount of chlorine containing plastics etc. In the Red or Yellow bay waste stream, the most commonly encountered plastics are polyvinylchloride, polyethylene and polypropylene. In this study, the pyrolysis of hospital waste has been studied with particular reference to PVC, which contains chlorine. The chemical analysis has indicated that H/sub 2/O or air must be added during the pyrolysis of PVC to prevent the formation of free solid carbon. By injecting steam into the first chamber, operating between 1000 degrees C and 1500 degrees C, carbon or soot is inhibited as the residue in the form of ash falls to the bottom. The off-gas passes to the second chamber where air may be added to provide oxidation and combustion. Operational efficiency of approximately 60% indicates a maximum input energy of 2-4 kWh/kg. Quenching of the output gases from the second chamber to around 100 degrees C is followed by alkaline scrubbing and filtering before venting with excess air to atmosphere.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High repetition rate generator for pulsed capacitively coupled discharges
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: There has been an increasing realisation that the intense chemical activity generated by nonthermal electrical breakdown phenomena may be exploited either as a mechanism for the destruction of gaseous waste materials or as the basis for an effective chemical synthesis technique. In this report the authors discuss some of the characteristics which a discharge suitable for this application may have and some of the efforts to realise these concepts in the laboratory. The work has concentrated on one particular form of nonthermal discharge, namely the dielectric barrier discharge, or silent discharge, and the development of a pulse generator suitable for driving such a discharge.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: The key to waste management is not what is to be done with waste or how much you pay someone to take it away, but minimising it at source. The authors describe how this can be achieved though the use of new processes which avoid or reduce the production of waste, or by recycling/converting waste into useful materials or energy during the process and within your factory. This aim poses significant challenges for science and engineering research.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A review of modelling of low pressure UV sources
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: Modelling has proved successful in assisting the understanding and development of low pressure discharges for a number of purposes. Here, the author describes how this provides the promise of application to UV sources for sterilisation. In order to achieve this goal, however, it will be necessary to address the particular problems facing each application, in order to determine the benefits which might be gained from the introduction of new technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radio frequency and microwave processing of wastes
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: Important developments have taken place in the use of radio frequency and microwave energy to process industrial, nuclear, medical and municipal waste materials. The principles of these techniques, together with applications, are outlined in this paper.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plasma pyrolysis: the destruction of toxic liquid wastes
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: The authors discuss the principles of plasma processes for treatment of waste materials. They then describe in general the different types of plasma reactors or torches used. They then describe in more detail the design of a plasma reactor for toxic liquid chemical waste treatment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plasma and electrical systems in glass manufacturing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electro-Technologies for Waste Processing and Purification
abstract: Glass has an advantage over the majority of recyclable packaging materials as recycling is simply a case of reheating until molten, then reforming. In general there is no degradation in the quality of the final product as is the case with many recycled products. It produces very few by-products (besides those generated by the heat source). Glass is also a reusable packaging material, being easy to clean and sterilise for use as food and drink containers. This presentation is concerned with the use of electrical heating as a means of melting glass, or as a means of aiding the melting of glass in conventional fossil fuel melters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
